pages.x: Since the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel had held Egypt's Sinai desert and Syria's Golan Heights. Egypt's president, Anwar Sadat, could not win them back by talking, and planned a war with Syria to break the deadlock. Israel's leaders, sure that the Arab armies would not dare to attack, missed the warnings.

At two in the afternoon of 6 October 1973, Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish year, Egyptian guns opened fire along the Suez Canal. Troops crossed in rubber boats, blasted gaps in the sand wall on the far bank with water cannon, and overran Israel's forts. In the north, Syrian tanks poured onto the Golan.

That morning the prime minister, Golda Meir, had decided not to strike first, so that the world could not blame Israel. Its reserves, called up from synagogues and homes, rushed to the fronts. In the first days Israel's leaders feared for the country, and the United States began a great airlift of arms.

On the Golan a few Israeli tank crews held off hundreds of Syrian tanks, in a place later called the Valley of Tears. By 10 October Israel had thrown the Syrians back to where they had started, and it pushed on toward Damascus, where Iraqi and Jordanian forces joined the fight.

In the south, Egyptian infantry with new Soviet anti-tank missiles smashed the first Israeli counterattacks. But on 14 October a great Egyptian tank attack failed, and the next night Ariel Sharon's division forced a crossing of the canal, amid savage fighting at a place called the Chinese Farm.

Israeli tanks spread out on the far bank and cut off Egypt's Third Army. The Soviet Union threatened to send in troops, and the United States put its nuclear forces on alert. Under pressure from both superpowers, a ceasefire took hold on 25 October.

In under three weeks more than 2,500 Israelis were killed, and many more Egyptians and Syrians, perhaps 10,000 or more. In Israel the shock brought down Golda Meir's government. Egypt celebrates the crossing of 6 October as a victory that restored Arab pride.
pages.of: Israelis killed, and far more Arabs

pages.x: To punish the United States and others who backed Israel, the Arab oil states cut their production and stopped selling oil to them. The price of oil quadrupled, queues formed at petrol stations in the West, and the world economy slid into recession.

The war gave Sadat the standing to make peace. In 1977 he flew to Jerusalem and spoke to Israel's parliament, and in 1979 Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty, under which Israel gave back the whole of Sinai. In 1981 Sadat was killed by Islamist soldiers during a parade.

The war ended Israel's belief that it could not be surprised, and gave Egypt back its pride. It brought the oil shock of the 1970s, and opened the way to the first peace between Israel and an Arab state, a peace that has held ever since.
pts: A surprise attack on Yom Kippur, 1973
Israel recovered and crossed the canal
It led to peace between Egypt and Israel
